title: Benchmarking Imbalance Measures Using Correlation and Data Complexity Analyses
author: Pivin-Bachler, van den Broek

steps.title: Open project in VS Code
steps.instruction: Open the repository folder containing main.py and main_functions.py in Visual Studio Code (VS Code). The script is interactive and will display results in the terminal.

steps.title: Set synthetic distribution parameters
steps.instruction: Edit main.py: on line 23 set `action = 'synth_data'`; on line 24 set `eval = 'f1'` or `eval = 'gmean'` to choose the performance metric; on line 25 set `N = 100` to run each scenario 100 times; on line 26 set `scenarios = 'a'`, `'b'`, or `'c'` to run a single scenario (default runs all three).

steps.title: Run synthetic distribution correlation
steps.instruction: In the terminal, execute `python ./main.py`. The program will display the current trial, then show Pearson (PCC) and Spearman (SRCC) correlation results for each imbalance measure. Press **Enter** to advance to the next measure (or comment out the `input()` call on line 1104 of main_functions.py to show all at once).

substeps.instruction: Press Enter after each measure (or comment input() on line 1104)

steps.title: Set synthetic feature parameters
steps.instruction: Edit main.py: on line 23 set `action = 'synth_ft'`; keep the same `eval` setting as step 2; keep `N = 100` on line 25; optionally set `scenarios = 'a'`, `'b'`, or `'c'` on line 26 to run a single feature‑component scenario.

steps.title: Run synthetic feature correlation
steps.instruction: In the terminal, run `python ./main.py`. Results are shown sequentially per imbalance measure; advance with **Enter** (or comment the `input()` call as above).

substeps.instruction: Press Enter after each measure (or comment input())

steps.title: Plot synthetic distribution trends
steps.instruction: Edit main.py: on line 23 set `action = 'synth_data_plot'`; then run `python ./main.py` to generate and display figures for the three data‑distribution scenarios. Close each figure with the **q** key to continue.

steps.title: Plot synthetic feature trends
steps.instruction: Edit main.py: on line 23 set `action = 'synth_ft_plot'`; then run `python ./main.py` to generate figures for the three feature‑component scenarios. Close each figure with **q**.

steps.title: Fast‑run synthetic minimal example
steps.instruction: For a quick demonstration, set `N = 1` on line 25 of main.py, then execute steps 1‑4 (set parameters, run correlation for distribution and features, and plot) using `python ./main.py`.

steps.title: Set real‑data correlation parameters
steps.instruction: Edit main.py: on line 23 set `action = 'real_data'`; on line 24 set `eval = 'f1'` or `eval = 'gmean'`; keep the default classifier list on line 101: `clfs = ['SVM', 'LDA', 'RF', 'kNN', 'MLP']`. To use a subset, replace the list on line 101 (e.g., `clfs = ['SVM', 'RF']`). Timing per classifier: SVM ≈ 1 h 42 min, LDA ≈ 3 min, RF ≈ 5 min, kNN ≈ 4 min, MLP ≈ 36 min.

steps.title: Run real‑data correlation
steps.instruction: Execute `python ./main.py` in the terminal. The program reports Pearson and Spearman correlations per imbalance measure for each classifier. Press **Enter** to move to the next classifier (or comment the `input()` call on line 1104).

substeps.instruction: Press Enter after each classifier (or comment input())

steps.title: Plot real‑data results
steps.instruction: Edit main.py: on line 23 set `action = 'real_data_plot'`; ensure the same `eval` setting as in step 8 and the same classifier list on line 110; then run `python ./main.py`. Quantitative results appear in the terminal; regression‑line figures appear sequentially—press **Enter** to open each figure and **q** to close it.

substeps.instruction: Press Enter to open figure, then 'q' to close

steps.title: Fast‑run real minimal example
steps.instruction: Reduce the classifier list to a single classifier (e.g., `clfs = ['LDA']` on line 101) and the same on line 110, then run steps 8 and 10 using `python ./main.py`.

steps.title: Set data complexity parameters
steps.instruction: Edit main.py: on line 23 set `action = 'complexity'`; on line 24 set `eval` as in step 2; on line 123 set `clf` to one of `SVM`, `LDA`, `RF`, `kNN`, or `MLP`. Ensure that lines 124 and 125 have matching values for `classif` and `eval_method`.

steps.title: Run data complexity analysis
steps.instruction: Run `python ./main.py`. For each data‑complexity measure the script prints the correlation and p‑value with classification performance and with each imbalance measure (order: IR, Adj‑IR, C1, C2, ID, LRID, IF, SIMBA).

steps.title: Fast‑run complexity minimal example
steps.instruction: Comment out all but the first three dataset names in the `l_datasets` list on line 1112 of main_functions.py, then run steps 12 and 13 with `python ./main.py`.

substeps.instruction: Keep only first three entries in l_datasets (line 1112)

description: Data is the fuel of machine learning. With imbalanced data, models struggle to learn patterns for the minority classes. Despite its prevalence in real-world data, imbalance is frequently overlooked or handled with an inadequate method. Indeed, methods to alleviate the impact of imbalance exist, but the choice of method to apply depends on the extent of imbalance. Seven imbalance measures were developed – namely, the imbalance ratio (IR), the adjusted IR (Adj-IR),2 the entropy of class proportions (C1),3,4 the multiclass imbalance ratio (C2),4,5 the imbalance degree (ID),6 the likelihood ratio imbalance degree (LRID),7 and the imbalance factor (IF)8 – but all present limitations. From this observation, the Status of IMBAlance (SIMBA) was created.1 Our protocol shows how to critically review these seven measures, evaluate their performance, and compare them to SIMBA. Contrary to other existing imbalance measures, SIMBA considers data distribution and data overlap, both crucial elements to estimate the impact of imbalance on classification difficulty. More specifically, for data distribution, SIMBA includes a comparison between the actual distribution of a dataset and a perfectly balanced distribution, and incorporates the correlation between features and class labels to assess data overlap. SIMBA can be applied to datasets with any number of classes, features, and samples, making it a robust and generalizable measure.1 Imbalance measures are benchmarked via correlation analysis with classification performance; first, on synthetic data to study trends in controlled scenarios, then, on real data to assess performance under more complex conditions. Further, as imbalance measures represent only one aspect of data complexity,4 a data complexity analysis is performed to evaluate how well these measures indicate classification difficulty relative to other complexity measures.
